title: Scheider ends five-year wait as Wehrlein seals DTM title
dek: Timo Scheider won Race 1 at Hockenheim by 2.875 seconds after taking the lead from pole-sitter Maxime Martin, while Pascal Wehrlein’s eighth place made him champion with one race to spare.

chapters.title: A title that needed only a podium
text: The 2015 DTM season reached its ninth and last round at Hockenheim in October with the drivers’ title all but decided. Pascal Wehrlein, in the gooix/Original-Teile Mercedes-AMG, arrived on 165 points, 37 clear of Edoardo Mortara and 38 ahead of Mattias Ekström, with Bruno Spengler 46 behind. Only two races, and so 50 points, remained, and the sums favoured the Mercedes driver heavily. A podium finish in either race would end the contest, and even a Saturday without points against a win for Ekström would still have left him 13 ahead.

A record was at stake as well. Wehrlein would turn 21 on Sunday, and a title this weekend would make him the youngest champion in DTM history. Mortara and Ekström, both in Audis, needed big results and a Wehrlein failure, while Spengler’s BMW was a long shot. Beyond the drivers’ crown, BMW led the manufacturers’ standings, which gave the weekend a second storyline. Saturday’s race was the 17th of the season’s 18, run over 40 minutes plus one lap on the 4.574-kilometre circuit.

chapters.title: Martin takes pole as the title contenders struggle
text: Maxime Martin put the BMW M4 of Team RMG on pole with a lap of 1m32.637s, 0.074s faster than Timo Scheider’s Audi from Team Phoenix. Miguel Molina’s Audi from Abt Sportsline was third on 1m32.726s, and Paul di Resta was fourth in the Silberpfeil Energy Mercedes, the quickest of the Mercedes drivers. Martin said he had not expected the car to be so strong, but that a lap free of traffic made the difference.

The session was extremely tight. Jamie Green (1m32.790s), Mike Rockenfeller (1m32.793s), Ekström (1m32.795s) and Tom Blomqvist (1m32.808s) filled the next four places, Mortara was ninth and Lucas Auer tenth, and the first ten cars were covered by 0.191s.

For the title contenders it was a poor day. Ekström, seventh, and Mortara, ninth, were the best placed of them, while Wehrlein managed only 13th, 0.255s off the pole time, and said he needed a good start and a strong long run to reach the points from there. Spengler, 18th, saw his slim chances shrink further. Paffett was 12th, Marco Wittmann, the reigning champion, only 16th, and Christian Vietoris was last on the grid in 24th.

chapters.title: All three title rivals stumble
text: Martin got away well from pole, but Molina bogged down behind him, and so did Ekström, whose slow getaway bunched up the midfield. Wehrlein dropped from 13th to 16th on the first lap, and Ekström was 18th. Mortara’s race went wrong in a first-lap clash with his Audi stablemate Molina, which punctured a tyre and sent him into the pits.

Spengler touched Adrien Tambay on the opening lap and earned a drive-through penalty for it, while Tambay was the first to retire, after a single lap. Scheider, second on the grid, closed on Martin and took the lead from him out of the hairpin in the early laps. On lap three Ekström was turned around at the hairpin by Robert Wickens’s Mercedes.

chapters.title: Wehrlein climbs while Mortara unravels
text: A clash between Paffett and Molina brought out the safety car. It ended Paffett’s race on lap three, while Molina carried on and was classified 17th, and Augusto Farfus was also out after four laps. When the field was released, Wehrlein began to work his way up, fighting hard with BMW’s Martin Tomczyk before moving into the top ten, and Green got past Martin to take second place.

Mortara, back out after his stop, passed Ekström but then spun Timo Glock’s BMW at the Sachs corner. A drive-through penalty followed, and the Italian was out after 17 laps. Glock lost two laps and was classified 18th, while Spengler, serving his own penalty, finished 19th and six laps down.

chapters.title: Scheider wins, Wehrlein is champion
text: Scheider, a two-time champion, kept his lead to the flag and won by 2.875s from Green, his first victory since October 2010. His quickest lap was a 1m34.364s on lap eight. Martin held off di Resta for third, 3.756s behind the winner and 1.1s ahead of the Mercedes, with Rockenfeller fifth, Wittmann sixth after starting 16th, and Blomqvist seventh.

The title was settled behind them. Wehrlein passed António Félix da Costa for eighth late on, and Ekström, who had recovered to ninth, was left 40 points adrift with only 25 on offer. Ekström took ninth by passing Vietoris and then, on the last lap, da Costa and Maximilian Götz, who took the final point in tenth. Wehrlein took four points for eighth, finished 22.034s behind the winner and ended the afternoon on 169, then celebrated with doughnuts in front of the Mercedes grandstand. He said he realised he was champion as he crossed the line.

Scheider said it was a great feeling to be back on top after such a hard season, and Audi’s Dieter Gass said the car had been the strongest again but the championship had still got away. BMW still led Audi by 56 in the manufacturers’ standings with one race to go.

facts.t: Title with a race to spare
facts.v: Wehrlein’s eighth place left him on 169 points, 40 clear of Ekström with only 25 available on Sunday, and made him the youngest champion in DTM history.
